title: Physics Horizons: A Conceptual Tour
subject: Horizons
summary: A parallel taste of the advanced physics to come, taken alongside the algebra and precalculus refresher. It uses only algebra, ratios, powers of ten and simple geometry, and still reasons honestly with real numbers: how physicists think and estimate, special relativity from light clocks, the quantum world (photons, matter waves, uncertainty, spin, entanglement), forces and the Standard Model, gravity and spacetime, and the history of the universe including where chemistry's elements come from. Each unit names the later course that makes it rigorous. Chemistry hooks run throughout (bond energies, photochemistry, NMR, PET, mass defects, nucleosynthesis).

units.title: How Physicists Think
units.summary: The habits that carry through every later unit: models with a domain, units and dimensional analysis, Fermi estimation, and scaling laws; made rigorous in M0 (estimation, dimensional analysis) and P1 Mechanics.

lessons.title: Models, Units and Dimensional Analysis
objectives: Explain what a physical model is (an idealization with a stated domain of validity) and judge whether a failed prediction means discarding the model or leaving its domain, using the ideal gas law at high pressure as the example.
Use dimensional analysis to check an equation and to derive the form of a relation, such as the pendulum period T proportional to sqrt(L/g), without solving any differential equation.
Carry units through a calculation and convert with powers of ten, including the chemist's energy units (J, eV, kJ/mol; kT at room temperature is about 25 meV).

demoIdeas: Pendulum dimension lab: pick which of L, g, m and amplitude the period may depend on; the demo lists the dimensionless combinations that exist and shows the single combination with units of time, then overlays measured periods for lengths from 10 cm to 10 m.
Unit juggler: drag a quantity (a bond enthalpy, a photon, a thermal energy) between J, eV, kJ/mol and kT at 298 K and see every conversion update with powers of ten.

lessons.title: Estimation and Powers of Ten
objectives: Break an unfamiliar quantity into factors you can estimate (a Fermi estimate), carry the result in powers of ten, and state how uncertain it is.
Estimate molecular-scale counts with Avogadro's number and PV = nRT: molecules in a breath, in a drop of water, in the atmosphere.
Explain why independent factor-of-3 errors partly cancel in a product, and use two independent routes to the same number as a sanity check.
keyEquations: \text{typical error of a product of }n\text{ factors}\sim f^{\sqrt n}

lessons.title: Scaling Laws: Why Size Changes Everything
objectives: Show that lengths, areas and volumes scale as L, L^2 and L^3, and use this to explain why surface-to-volume ratio falls as 1/L (cooling, strength-to-weight, finely divided catalysts).
Make a scaling argument that predicts what happens when an object is shrunk or enlarged (why ants are strong and giants are impossible, why a drop cools faster than a lake).
Place nature on a ladder of length scales from the nucleus (1e-15 m) to the observable universe (1e26 m) and say which kind of physics governs each rung.

Cutting a cube: slice a 1 cm cube into smaller and smaller cubes and watch total surface area, the fraction of atoms on the surface and the cooling time update.

units.title: Special Relativity with Algebra
units.summary: Einstein's postulates, simultaneity, light clocks, time dilation, length contraction and E = mc^2 with mass defects in nuclei and chemistry, using only algebra and the Pythagorean theorem; made rigorous in P3 (Lorentz transformations) and later P5 and S3.

lessons.title: Einstein's Postulates and the Relativity of Simultaneity
objectives: State Einstein's two postulates and explain why they conflict with Galilean velocity addition (a flashlight on a moving train) and what the Michelson-Morley null result adds.
Use the train-and-lightning thought experiment to show that two events simultaneous in one frame are not simultaneous in another, and decide which comes first for a given direction of motion.
Estimate the size of the effect with the small-speed formula for the time offset, and say why we never notice it in daily life.

lessons.title: Light Clocks and Time Dilation
objectives: Derive Delta t = gamma Delta t0 with gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) from a light clock using only the Pythagorean theorem and the constancy of c.
Compute gamma for a given v/c, use the low-speed approximation gamma ~ 1 + v^2/2c^2 for quick estimates, and sketch gamma(v) up to v -> c.
Explain why the effect is symmetric (each observer finds the other's clock slow) and what proper time means.

lessons.title: Length Contraction and the Cosmic-Ray Muon
objectives: Use the muon's 2.2 microsecond lifetime to show that without relativity a cosmic-ray muon made 15 km up would essentially never reach the ground, and compute the survival fraction with time dilation.
State length contraction L = L0/gamma along the direction of motion (none perpendicular), derive it by timing the same trip in two frames, and tell the muon's-eye-view story.
Explain why both accounts give the same survival fraction: the frames disagree about durations and lengths but agree on what happens.

lessons.title: E = mc^2, Mass Defects and Chemical Energy
objectives: Explain with the light-in-a-box argument (a photon of energy E carries momentum E/c) why energy has inertia, m = E/c^2, and what 'rest energy' means.

Compute the energy released from a mass defect, and compare scales: a chemical bond (about 1 eV per atom, mass change near 1 part in 1e10) versus a nuclear reaction (about 1 MeV per nucleon, near 1 part in 1e3).
Explain why conservation of mass is only approximately true in chemistry, using combustion of methane as a worked example.

units.title: The Quantum World
units.summary: Photons, matter waves, the double slit, uncertainty, standing-wave quantization, spin and the Pauli principle, and entanglement, with the case for why chemistry needs all of it; made rigorous in P6 Quantum Mechanics (with M3 linear algebra and M5 methods).

lessons.title: Photons and the Photoelectric Effect
objectives: Explain why the wave picture of light fails for the photoelectric effect (threshold frequency, no delay, kinetic energy independent of intensity) and how E = hf accounts for each observation.

Compute photon energies with E = hc/lambda (about 1240 eV nm divided by wavelength) and decide whether a photon can eject an electron or break a bond; chemistry hook: why photochemistry needs UV and visible light does not break C-C bonds.
Use K_max = hf - phi to find stopping potentials and read Planck's constant from the slope of a K_max versus frequency line.

lessons.title: Matter Waves and the Double Slit
objectives: Compute the de Broglie wavelength lambda = h/p for electrons, molecules (C60) and everyday objects, and say when wave behaviour is observable by comparing lambda with the size of the slit or lattice spacing.
Describe the double-slit experiment with particles sent one at a time: single localized hits build an interference pattern, so probabilities come from adding amplitudes and then squaring.
Explain why determining which slit the particle used destroys the fringes, and relate electron and neutron diffraction to structure determination in chemistry.

lessons.title: The Uncertainty Principle and the Size of Atoms
objectives: State Delta x Delta p >= hbar/2 as a property of waves (a narrow packet needs many wavelengths), not a limit of instruments, and use it to estimate confinement energies.

Estimate the size and energy of hydrogen by balancing confinement kinetic energy hbar^2/(2 m r^2) against Coulomb attraction; completing the square gives the Bohr radius and -13.6 eV, and shows what stops the electron from falling into the nucleus.
Compare confinement energies for an electron in an atom (eV) and a nucleon in a nucleus (MeV) and explain the ratio.

Atom-size balance: plot confinement energy, Coulomb energy and their sum versus radius; the minimum lands at 0.53 angstrom and -13.6 eV, and a mass slider shows how the atom would change for a heavier or lighter electron.

lessons.title: Standing Waves, Quantization and Orbitals
objectives: Show that quantized energies come from fitting standing waves into a confined region: for a box lambda_n = 2L/n and E_n = n^2 h^2/(8 m L^2), with the number of nodes rising with energy.

Apply the box model to conjugated dyes: predict how the HOMO-LUMO absorption wavelength moves to the red as the chain lengthens (chemistry: colour of polyenes and beta-carotene), and note where the model is crude.
Describe hydrogen orbitals as three-dimensional standing waves labelled n, l, m, count radial nodes (n - l - 1) and connect shell structure to the energies -13.6 eV/n^2.

lessons.title: Spin, the Pauli Principle and the Basis of NMR
objectives: Describe spin-1/2 as an intrinsic two-valued property revealed by Stern-Gerlach splitting, and explain why it cannot be a literally spinning ball.
State the Pauli exclusion principle and use it with the (n, l, m) orbital counting to build the 2, 8, 8, 18 rhythm of the periodic table and explain why a filled shell is chemically quiet.

Explain spin resonance: a spin in field B has two energy levels split by hf = gamma hbar B, a radio-frequency photon flips it, and the tiny Boltzmann population difference (about 30 ppm at 400 MHz) sets NMR's sensitivity.

lessons.title: Entanglement and Bell's Inequality
objectives: Describe an entangled spin pair (singlet): each outcome alone is random 50/50, yet the two outcomes are perfectly anti-correlated along any shared axis.

Derive by counting (Wigner-d'Espagnat) that any local 'hidden instruction' model obeys P(a+,c+) <= P(a+,b+) + P(b+,c+), then show that the quantum prediction at 0, 60 and 120 degrees breaks it by a factor of 1.5.
State what Bell violation rules out (local pre-existing values) and what it does not (it carries no usable signal faster than light); chemistry hook: singlet and triplet electron pairs.

units.title: Nuclei, Particles and the Standard Model
units.summary: The four forces and their carriers, quarks and the origin of mass, the weak force and neutrinos, antimatter and PET, and the Higgs at a conceptual level; made rigorous in S1 Particle Physics and, for the field-theory machinery, S4 Quantum Field Theory.

lessons.title: Four Forces, Their Carriers and Their Ranges
objectives: List the four fundamental interactions with their relative strengths (strong 1, electromagnetic 1/137, weak ~1e-6, gravity ~1e-39 between protons) and the everyday phenomenon each controls, including which hold nuclei and atoms together.
Explain force as exchange of a carrier and use the uncertainty principle (borrow mc^2 for a time hbar/mc^2) to estimate range R ~ hbar c/(mc^2): pion 1.4 fm, W boson 0.0025 fm, photon infinite.
Compare gravity and electricity between two protons (ratio ~1e36) and explain why gravity still wins for planets and stars.

lessons.title: Quarks and the Origin of the Proton's Mass
objectives: Describe protons and neutrons as uud and udd bound states (charges +2/3 and -1/3) and mesons as quark-antiquark pairs, and check charge sums for allowed combinations.
Explain colour confinement qualitatively: pulling quarks apart stores energy in the strong field until a new quark-antiquark pair appears, so jets of hadrons emerge and free quarks are never seen.
Use E = mc^2 to show that about 99% of the proton's mass is strong-force field and kinetic energy, not quark rest mass, so nearly all of the mass of atoms (and of you) has this origin.

lessons.title: The Weak Force and Neutrinos
objectives: Explain why beta decay (n -> p + e- + antineutrino) seemed to violate energy conservation (continuous electron spectrum) and how Pauli's neutrino fixed it; state that the weak force changes quark flavour (d -> u via W-).
Estimate neutrino numbers and rarity: about 6e10 solar neutrinos per cm^2 per second pass through you and almost none interact, because neutrinos feel only the weak force and gravity.

State what neutrino oscillation implies (nonzero neutrino masses, tiny but real) and why it counts as evidence beyond the original Standard Model; chemistry hook: radiocarbon dating and K-40 in the body are weak decays.

lessons.title: Antimatter and PET Scans
objectives: Explain how combining relativity (E^2 = p^2c^2 + m^2c^4 allows E = +/-) with quantum mechanics led Dirac to antiparticles with equal mass and opposite charge, confirmed by the positron in 1932.
Compute the annihilation signal: e+ e- -> two 511 keV photons emitted back to back (one photon would violate momentum conservation), and the pair-production threshold of 1.022 MeV.
Explain how a PET scan works, from F-18 FDG (half-life 110 min) beta-plus decay through positron annihilation to coincidence detection, and why the half-life matters for radiochemistry.

lessons.title: The Higgs Field and the Standard Model at a Glance
objectives: Lay out the Standard Model inventory: 6 quarks and 6 leptons in three generations, the carriers (photon, gluons, W, Z) and the Higgs, and say which few particles (u, d, e) make up ordinary matter.

Explain the Higgs mechanism conceptually (a field with nonzero value everywhere that gives mass to particles that couple to it) and why a massless electron would give no atoms, since the atom's size scales as 1/m_e.
State what the Standard Model leaves unexplained: dark matter, gravity, the matter-antimatter imbalance, the origin of neutrino masses, and why there are three generations.

units.title: Gravity and Spacetime
units.summary: The equivalence principle, curved spacetime, gravitational time dilation and GPS, black holes and gravitational waves, with real numbers from weak-field algebra; made rigorous in S3 General Relativity (which needs P4 and the tensor methods of M5).

lessons.title: The Equivalence Principle and Curved Spacetime
objectives: State the equivalence principle (inertial and gravitational mass are equal, so a freely falling lab is locally indistinguishable from empty space) and use an accelerating-elevator thought experiment to show that light must bend in a gravitational field.

Explain gravity as geometry: freely falling objects follow the straightest possible paths (geodesics) in curved spacetime, and tidal stretching between neighbouring paths is the measurable sign of curvature; state honestly where the rubber-sheet picture misleads.
Evaluate the light deflection by the Sun, delta = 4GM/(c^2 R) = 1.75 arcseconds, and say why Newtonian gravity gives half of that.

demoIdeas: Einstein elevator: toggle between a rocket accelerating in empty space and a lab resting on Earth, and trace a light beam and a dropped ball in each to see they match.

lessons.title: Gravitational Time Dilation and GPS
objectives: Explain with the accelerating-rocket argument why clocks higher in a gravitational field run faster, with fractional rate difference gh/c^2 near Earth.

Compute the two GPS corrections: speed makes satellite clocks slower by about 7 microseconds per day, altitude makes them faster by about 46 microseconds per day, net +38 microseconds per day, which would become an 11 km position error per day.
Interpret the size of the effect in other settings (a tower of 22.5 m, a centimetre-scale optical clock, the Earth's core versus surface) and say why it is a precision test, not a daily curiosity.

lessons.title: Black Holes: Horizons and Tidal Forces
objectives: Compute the Schwarzschild radius r_s = 2GM/c^2 (Sun 2.95 km, Earth 8.9 mm) and explain why the Newtonian escape-velocity argument gives the right number but hides the real physics, which is a horizon from which no future path leads out.
Contrast the infalling and distant views: the faller crosses the horizon in finite proper time, while the distant observer sees the faller's light redden and fade.

Show that average density inside the horizon falls as 1/M^2 (a 1e8 solar-mass hole is about as dense as water) and that tidal forces at the horizon fall with mass, and list the observational evidence (stellar-mass holes, Sgr A*, the EHT image).

demoIdeas: Black hole size and density: mass slider from 1 to 1e10 solar masses showing r_s, average density and the tidal acceleration across a 2 m body at the horizon.
Light cones near a horizon: draw cones tipping inward as you approach r_s so you can see why every future path from inside points to smaller r.

lessons.title: Gravitational Waves: LIGO's Whisper
objectives: Explain that accelerating masses make ripples in spacetime travelling at c that alternately stretch and squeeze distances by a fractional strain h = Delta L / L, and why only merging compact objects produce detectable waves.

Estimate the first detection (GW150914): strain about 1e-21 across 4 km gives Delta L about 4e-18 m, around 1/400 of a proton diameter, from about 3 solar masses of energy (E = Delta m c^2) radiated in a fraction of a second.

Explain how a Michelson-type interferometer with long arms and laser cavities reaches this sensitivity, what a rising-frequency chirp encodes, and how the neutron-star merger GW170817 linked gravitational waves to the production of gold (chemistry hook).

units.title: The Universe
units.summary: Expansion and the scale of things, the cosmic microwave background, nucleosynthesis and the origin of the chemical elements, and the dark matter and dark energy puzzles; made rigorous in S2 Astrophysics & Cosmology (with P3 and P7).

lessons.title: An Expanding Universe and the Scale of Things
objectives: Explain Hubble's law v = H0 d as the signature of uniform expansion (every observer sees the same law, with no centre) and cosmological redshift 1 + z = a_now/a_then as the stretching of wavelengths.
Compute the Hubble time 1/H0 (about 14 billion years for H0 = 70 km/s/Mpc) as a rough age scale and estimate distance from redshift for small z.

Place objects on the cosmic ladder (light-minutes to the Sun, light-years to stars, 100,000 ly for the Milky Way, 46 billion ly to the edge of the observable universe), and describe how the distance ladder (parallax, Cepheids, supernovae) is chained.

lessons.title: The Cosmic Microwave Background
objectives: Explain the CMB as relic light released at recombination (T about 3000 K, z about 1100) that has been stretched by expansion to 2.725 K, and use T = T0 (1 + z).

Explain why atoms formed at 3000 K (kT about 0.26 eV) rather than at 13.6 eV: there are about 1e9 photons per baryon, so the Planck tail still ionizes hydrogen until the universe is far cooler (a Boltzmann-factor argument).
Interpret the anisotropies: the 3.4 mK dipole from our motion (v/c times T) and the 1 part in 100,000 ripples that seeded galaxies.

lessons.title: Nucleosynthesis: Where Chemistry's Elements Come From
objectives: Explain Big Bang nucleosynthesis: the neutron-proton ratio freezes out via the Boltzmann factor exp(-1.29 MeV/kT), decays to about 1/7 before deuterium forms, and nearly all neutrons end up in helium-4, giving a helium mass fraction Y = 2x/(1+x) = 0.25.

Explain why the Big Bang made essentially nothing heavier than lithium (no stable nuclei at A = 5 and 8, falling density) and where the rest of the periodic table is made: stellar fusion up to iron, then neutron capture in supernovae, merging neutron stars and giant stars.

Use the binding-energy curve to explain why fusion releases energy only up to iron and why this matters for the elements in your body (chemistry hook: C, N, O made in stars; the same Boltzmann factor appears in Arrhenius kinetics).

lessons.title: Dark Matter and Dark Energy
objectives: Use v^2 = GM/r to show that planetary speeds fall as 1/sqrt(r) while galaxy rotation curves stay flat, implying enclosed mass M(<r) = v^2 r/G growing with r, and list independent evidence (cluster dynamics, lensing, CMB peaks, big bang nucleosynthesis limits on ordinary matter).
State what dark matter must be like (gravitates, does not shine, not ordinary atoms, slow-moving) and list the leading candidates and null searches, plus an honest mention of modified gravity.

Explain how distant Type Ia supernovae revealed accelerating expansion (dark energy), quote the cosmic budget (about 5% ordinary matter, 27% dark matter, 68% dark energy), and say what needs later mathematics.
